definition: A durable buffer in which producers add messages and consumers take them, decoupling the two sides in time and absorbing load spikes.
A messaging pattern in which publishers send messages to a topic and every subscriber of that topic receives its own copy.
A named channel or stream of messages to which producers publish and from which consumers read.
An ordered, append-only slice of a topic; ordering is guaranteed only within a partition, and partitions let consumers read in parallel.
A set of consumers that share a topic's partitions so each message is processed by exactly one member of the group.
A consumer's position in a partition's log; committing offsets lets it resume after a restart and enables replay.
A distributed, partitioned, replicated commit log used for high-throughput event streaming, with retention that lets consumers replay history.
A message broker that routes messages through exchanges to queues using flexible rules and deletes them once acknowledged.
A fully managed message queue service offering standard queues (at-least-once, best-effort order) and FIFO queues with ordering and deduplication.
A side queue that receives messages that repeatedly failed processing, so they can be inspected and redriven without blocking healthy traffic.
A message that can never be processed successfully, for example because of malformed data, and would be retried forever without a retry limit.
The promise about the order in which messages are consumed; most systems guarantee order only per key or partition, not globally.
A delivery guarantee in which a message is delivered zero or one times: no duplicates, but it may be lost.
A delivery guarantee in which a message is delivered one or more times: it is never lost but may be duplicated, so consumers must be idempotent.
The effect of processing each message once, achieved in practice by at-least-once delivery combined with idempotent or transactional handling rather than true single delivery.
Continuously computing over an unbounded flow of events as they arrive, instead of in periodic batch jobs.
Grouping stream events into finite windows (tumbling, sliding or session) by time so aggregates such as counts can be computed.
Reading a database's change log to emit each insert, update and delete as an event that other systems can consume.
A shared channel through which services publish and subscribe to events, so producers do not need to know their consumers.
A flat store of immutable objects addressed by key, with rich metadata and very high durability, such as Amazon S3.
Raw fixed-size blocks presented as a disk to a single machine, giving low-latency random access for databases and operating systems.
A shared hierarchical file system with directories and POSIX-like semantics that many machines can mount, such as NFS.
A binary large object: an opaque chunk of unstructured data such as an image or video, stored as a single object.
A time-limited URL, signed with credentials, that lets a client upload to or download from object storage directly without proxying through your servers.
Uploading a large object as independent parts that can be sent in parallel and retried individually, then assembled by the storage service.
Splitting data into fragments plus parity pieces so the original can be rebuilt from any sufficient subset, giving durability with less storage overhead than full copies.
The probability that stored data is not lost over time, usually expressed in nines per year and achieved through replication and backups.
The fraction of time a system is able to serve requests correctly, often stated in nines (99.9% allows about 8.8 hours of downtime a year).
A service level indicator: a measured quantity describing service quality, such as the fraction of requests answered successfully under 300 ms.
A service level objective: the target value for an SLI over a period, such as 99.9% of requests succeed over 30 days.
A service level agreement: a contract with customers that states the promised service level and the remedy, usually credits, when it is missed.
The amount of unreliability an SLO permits (100% minus the target); teams spend it on changes and pause risky releases when it runs out.
Mean time to recovery: the average time from a failure starting until service is restored.
Mean time between failures: the average operating time between one failure and the next for a repairable component.
Recovery point objective: the maximum amount of data loss, measured in time, that is acceptable after a disaster.
Recovery time objective: the maximum acceptable time to restore service after a disaster.
The plans and infrastructure for restoring service and data after a major failure such as the loss of a data center or region.
Running a system in more than one geographic region to cut latency for distant users and survive a regional outage.
A setup in which several sites or nodes serve live traffic at the same time, using capacity fully and failing over with little disruption.
A setup in which a standby site or node stays idle until the active one fails, simpler to reason about but leaving capacity unused.
Deliberately injecting failures, such as killing instances or adding latency, to verify that a system tolerates them before real outages do.
The ability to understand a system's internal state from its outputs, built on logs, metrics and traces.
Recording discrete, timestamped events from a service, ideally as structured data, to reconstruct what happened during an incident.
Numeric measurements aggregated over time, such as request rate, error rate and latency percentiles, used for dashboards and alerts.
Following a single request across services by propagating a trace id and recording timed spans, to find where latency or errors arise.
Rolling a new version out to a small share of traffic first and expanding only if its metrics stay healthy.
Running two identical environments and switching traffic from the old (blue) to the new (green) at once, allowing instant rollback.
A runtime switch that enables or disables functionality without redeploying, used for gradual rollouts and quick kill switches.
An authorization framework that lets an application obtain limited access to a user's resources through access tokens, without handling the user's password.
An identity layer on top of OAuth 2.0 that adds an ID token so an application can learn who the user is, not only what they may access.
A JSON Web Token: a compact, signed set of claims that a server can verify without a database lookup; because it is hard to revoke it is given a short lifetime.
Server-side or token-based state that links a series of requests to one authenticated user, usually identified by a cookie.
Role-based access control: permissions are granted to roles and users get roles, which keeps authorization manageable as the user base grows.
Encrypting stored data on disks or in object storage so that stolen media or backups cannot be read without the keys.
Encrypting data while it moves across a network, normally with TLS, so eavesdroppers cannot read or alter it.
TLS in which both sides present certificates, so each service verifies the other's identity; common for service-to-service traffic.
A distributed denial-of-service attack that floods a service with traffic from many sources to exhaust bandwidth or resources; mitigated with CDNs, rate limits and scrubbing.
